doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Monk, the Army and learning the job
title: Interviewing Monk and buying him out of Prestige for Riverside
summary: His early Monk article led Monk to sign with Riverside after Keepnews paid back Prestige's $128 advance.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: in those days that I did not realize the impossibility of what I wisely set out to do, but on the spot it was a big, sprawling Greenwich Village studio living room, Monk and I went off into a corner disregarding all the other people there and I interviewed him for an article that appeared in the magazine. A number of years later when I had a fledgling record company and had heard the accurate rumor that Monk, who at that time was with Prestige, was very unhappy with where he was, they were not happy with him, he wasn’t selling records, at least he was a famous eccentric by that point, and they would be perfectly happy to get rid of him. But of course they wouldn’t have if they had known that another record company was interested. So we had a fairly clandestine meeting with Monk, sort of came to a gentleman’s agreement kind of situation, and what Prestige wanted was to be repaid not what — its royalty account was in the red, that’s always quite fictional — but the actual dollar amount that he had been over advanced by them which was $128 and change, so I gave him $130 and he went, actually the offices of Prestige were around the corner from the offices of Riverside in those days, he went around the corner and I still have in my possession — I insisted that he had to give me the original release letter, which had been prepared, saying your check for and then that was scratched out and cash was put in, a letter from Bob Weinstock to Thelonious Monk releasing him of his contractual obligations to Prestige. Monk then proceeded to sign with Riverside and in a very real sense that was the beginning of Riverside as a company to be taken seriously and it was, as far as I’m concerned, it was the beginning of my career as a jazz record producer. Now I had said previously to you that a lot of my life was accidental, that’s pretty damned accidental.
Well it’s almost like the fact that you were so new to it was to your advantage.

Well the interesting thing is that when we learned of the availability of, or potential availability of Monk, I had no idea that he would have any recollection of this whole initial encounter in light of that, but upon re-meeting him he proceeded to let us know he knew exactly who we were and he informed me that the article that I had written about him, not only obviously did he like it but he said it had been the first piece about him to ever appear in a national magazine. Well The Record Changer was a national magazine by courtesy. I suppose you could call it that, but the whole point was that it was the fact of my having done that bit of strange journalism that was the key thing. It meant that Monk remembered who I was, remembered me and the publication favorably and, you know, what the hell, was willing to take a chance with our scene.
